stories.headline: Kaumālapaʻu Harbor to begin limited operations Sunday for essential barge delivery
stories.summary: HDOT says the Lānaʻi harbor will accept a special interisland barge on September 13 while access remains restricted and land-side repairs continue.
stories.why_it_matters: Kaumālapaʻu is Lānaʻi’s primary commercial cargo facility, so limited reopening supports delivery of goods and fuel while keeping the damaged work area controlled.
body: The Hawaiʻi Department of Transportation says limited operations will begin at Kaumālapaʻu Harbor on Lānaʻi on Sunday, September 13, as crews continue repairs following Hurricane Lowell.
HDOT says underwater hazards will be removed from the waterway in time for an incoming barge. Young Brothers is scheduled to send a special interisland shipment carrying goods and fuel to Lānaʻi.

The harbor will remain closed to the public and to anyone who is not essential harbor personnel. HDOT says the restriction is needed so barge offloading and paving work can proceed safely in the limited space, with Maui Police assisting access control.

Limited operations do not mean all repairs are complete. Land-side work will continue for the coming weeks, including repairs around the pier apron. Residents should not enter the harbor area to watch the barge or inspect recovery work.

The practical takeaway for Lānaʻi residents is that an essential supply shipment is scheduled, but normal public access has not resumed. Future operating changes should be confirmed through HDOT’s official weather and transportation updates.

stories.headline: Kauaʻi asks residents to conserve water while pumps run on emergency generators
stories.summary: The Kauaʻi Department of Water says its islandwide conservation notice remains active and asks customers to limit use to essential needs to help prevent an outage.
stories.why_it_matters: Water systems have been restored, but emergency-powered pumping remains vulnerable during hurricane recovery; reducing demand helps preserve cooking, drinking, hygiene and sanitation service.
body: The Kauaʻi Department of Water is reminding customers that an islandwide water-conservation notice remains in effect as recovery from Hurricane Lowell continues. The department says water pumps are operating on emergency-powered generators and conserving water will help reduce the risk of a service outage.

Customers are asked to limit water use to essential needs, including cooking, drinking, personal hygiene, laundry and sanitation. The department also recommends turning off equipment that draws water automatically, such as irrigation systems and ice machines.

The County of Kauaʻi reported Saturday that the island’s water systems had been restored, but the conservation request remained in place. That means the notice is a demand-management precaution while generator-dependent pumping and broader infrastructure recovery continue.

The conservation notice is separate from any location-specific boil-water advisory. Residents should check the Department of Water’s service-outage page for the latest instructions affecting their own neighborhood rather than assume that an islandwide conservation request changes water-quality guidance.

The department says the notice will remain active until it is formally lifted. Water-service outages or leaks can be reported to 808-245-5444. Residents should continue following official county and Department of Water updates as power and pumping conditions change.

stories.headline: PAGASA: Localized thunderstorms possible across the Philippines on September 13
stories.summary: PAGASA forecasts partly cloudy to cloudy skies with isolated rainshowers or thunderstorms across most of the country, with easterlies affecting the far north.
stories.why_it_matters: Families and travelers should expect mostly localized weather but remain alert because severe thunderstorms can still trigger flash floods or landslides.
body: The Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical and Astronomical Services Administration says localized thunderstorms may bring isolated rainshowers across much of the Philippines on Sunday, September 13. The national forecast was issued at 4:00 a.m. Philippine time and describes partly cloudy to cloudy conditions for Metro Manila and most other areas.

PAGASA says easterlies are affecting Batanes and the Babuyan Islands, where isolated rainshowers or thunderstorms are also possible. For Metro Manila and the rest of the country, localized thunderstorms are the main weather driver rather than a single nationwide rain system.

Even when rain is isolated, PAGASA cautions that severe thunderstorms can produce flash floods or landslides. Conditions can vary sharply over short distances, so residents should check regional warnings and local government advisories before travel, outdoor events or trips through flood- and landslide-prone areas.

The agency forecasts light to moderate winds. Coastal waters are expected to be slight to moderate, at about 1.2 to 2.1 meters in Extreme Northern Luzon and roughly 0.6 to 1.5 meters elsewhere. Local marine bulletins should still be checked because thunderstorm conditions can change quickly.

For Hawaiʻi families coordinating with relatives or travelers in the Philippines, the practical takeaway is to plan for brief, localized downpours rather than assume uniform rain nationwide. Monitor PAGASA’s current forecast and regional advisories, and avoid flooded roads or unstable slopes if a strong thunderstorm develops.

stories.headline: Hawaiʻi conditionally clears Navy ʻAiea Hālawa drinking-water shaft for reactivation
stories.summary: The Hawaiʻi Department of Health says the Navy may reactivate the ʻAiea Hālawa Shaft only after required treatment, testing and advance customer notification conditions are met.
stories.why_it_matters: The decision affects the resilience of the Joint Base Pearl Harbor-Hickam water system, which serves about 93,000 users, while keeping monitoring and enforcement requirements in place.
body: The Hawaiʻi Department of Health has conditionally approved the Navy’s request to reactivate the ʻAiea Hālawa Shaft as a drinking-water source for the Joint Base Pearl Harbor-Hickam public water system. The department says the additional source is intended to improve system resilience by supplementing the Waiawa Shaft, which regulators had identified as a single-source vulnerability for a system serving about 93,000 users.

The approval is conditional, not an immediate or unrestricted return to service. DOH required granular activated carbon treatment, ion-exchange treatment and disinfection systems, along with sampling points for continued testing. The department said testing covered more than 50 contaminants, including PFAS and total petroleum hydrocarbons, and did not find them above applicable regulatory standards.

PFAS had been detected at the shaft in June 2024, so the Navy was also required to demonstrate that the installed treatment could remove those compounds. The Navy must operate the system under state and federal drinking-water laws and report within 24 hours any condition that could contaminate the source.

DOH emphasized that the Navy’s ʻAiea Hālawa Shaft is not the Navy’s Red Hill Shaft or the Honolulu Board of Water Supply’s Hālawa Shaft. The agency said the source is about two miles from the Red Hill facility and that a geologic barrier, the expected low pumping rate and continued pumping at the Red Hill Shaft make an effect on underground contamination unlikely under the approved conditions.

Before reactivation, the Navy must notify its customers and DOH at least 10 days in advance. DOH says it will continue monitoring groundwater data and may suspend or revoke the approval if conditions are not met or if a future public-health threat is identified. Readers served by the system should rely on official Navy and DOH notices for the actual start date and any customer instructions.

stories.headline: Kauaʻi recovery keeps Wailua traffic controls in place as emergency Hanalei access returns
stories.summary: HDOT says an emergency access lane has been restored at Hanalei Bridge, while debris-clearing work at the Wailua River Bridge continues through Friday with traffic controls in place.
stories.why_it_matters: Kauaʻi residents, workers and travelers should expect recovery-related delays even as access improves after Lowell.
body: Kauaʻi transportation recovery is moving forward after Hurricane Lowell, but drivers should still expect storm-related traffic controls Thursday. The Hawaiʻi Department of Transportation says crews have restored an emergency access lane on Kūhiō Highway at Hanalei Bridge, improving access to communities that had been affected by fallen poles and storm damage.

At the Wailua River Bridge, recovery work continues as crews clear debris from beneath the mauka bridge. HDOT has said this work will continue through Friday, September 11. During the operation, the mauka bridge is closed and the makai bridge is being used in a contraflow configuration so traffic can continue moving in both directions.

The normal southbound morning contraflow through the Wailua corridor is not operating during the recovery work. That means commuters who regularly depend on the special-use lane should allow additional travel time and watch for changing traffic patterns, workers and equipment near the bridge area.

HDOT is also continuing broader recovery work across Kauaʻi. The agency has been clearing trees and debris from state highways and coordinating access restoration in areas affected by Lowell. Port Allen remained closed in the agency’s latest transportation update, underscoring that storm recovery is still uneven across the island.

For PinoyLink Hawaiʻi readers traveling on Kauaʻi, the practical takeaway is that access is improving, but some routes are still operating under temporary recovery conditions. Check current HDOT notices before leaving, follow posted traffic controls, and avoid assuming that normal commute patterns have fully resumed simply because a roadway is open.

stories.headline: Hawaiian Electric begins shifting crews and equipment to support Kauaʻi recovery
stories.summary: Hawaiian Electric says nearly all Oʻahu customers affected by Lowell have been restored and its first team is due on Kauaʻi Thursday to assist with damage assessments and recovery support.
stories.why_it_matters: The utility response is moving toward Kauaʻi, where storm recovery remains active, while Oʻahu restoration is largely complete.
body: Hawaiian Electric is shifting personnel and equipment toward Kauaʻi as Hawaiʻi’s post-Lowell recovery enters a new phase. The utility said nearly all Oʻahu customers affected by Hurricane Lowell had been restored by Wednesday, allowing it to prepare teams to assist Kauaʻi Island Utility Cooperative with recovery work on Kauaʻi.

The first Hawaiian Electric team is scheduled to arrive on Kauaʻi Thursday to help with damage assessments and determine what supplies and equipment are needed. Additional trucks and equipment are expected to arrive by barge Friday. Hawaiian Electric serves Oʻahu, Maui County and Hawaiʻi Island, while Kauaʻi is served by the separate Kauaʻi Island Utility Cooperative, so the effort is a coordinated mutual-aid response rather than a transfer of utility control.

The deployment follows substantial restoration progress on Oʻahu. Earlier this week, Hawaiian Electric reported that crews had restored most customers affected by Lowell, with remaining outages concentrated in smaller pockets and some cases involving damage to privately owned electrical equipment. The company has cautioned that certain customers may need an electrician to repair customer-owned equipment before service can be safely reconnected.

For families on Kauaʻi, the arrival of outside crews and equipment should expand recovery capacity, but it does not establish a specific restoration time for every neighborhood. Damage assessments still determine what work is required, and local updates from Kauaʻi Island Utility Cooperative remain the most direct source for island-specific outage information.

For Oʻahu readers, the shift in resources is another sign that broad storm restoration there is nearing completion. Anyone still without power should continue using Hawaiian Electric’s official outage channels and should treat damaged electrical equipment and downed lines as hazardous until cleared by qualified personnel.

stories.headline: Oʻahu power restoration advances; about 440 customers remained out at 6:30 a.m.
stories.summary: Hawaiian Electric says crews restored another 1,060 Oʻahu customers overnight after Hurricane Lowell, leaving about 440 customers without power as of 6:30 a.m. Wednesday, mainly in Mākaha Valley and pockets of Honolulu and Windward Oʻahu.
stories.why_it_matters: The update shows substantial progress in Oʻahu recovery while giving remaining affected households a current utility estimate and practical restoration guidance.
body: Oʻahu’s post-Lowell power restoration moved substantially closer to completion Wednesday morning. Hawaiian Electric reported that crews restored electricity overnight to another 1,060 customers affected by Hurricane Lowell. As of 6:30 a.m. Wednesday, about 440 customers remained without power, primarily in Mākaha Valley and in smaller pockets of Honolulu and Windward Oʻahu.

The latest utility update is a major improvement from Tuesday night, when Hawaiian Electric reported roughly 1,500 Oʻahu customers still without service. Crews had already completed assessments and most repairs in West Oʻahu, including Nānākuli, Waiʻanae and Mākaha, after access improved. The company said assessments and repairs for the remaining affected areas were expected to be completed later Wednesday.

Restoration does not necessarily mean every individual property can be reconnected immediately. Hawaiian Electric cautioned that some customers may have damage to privately owned electrical equipment. Depending on the damage, a licensed electrician may need to make repairs before the utility can safely restore service to a home or business.

Customers who remain without electricity are advised by Hawaiian Electric to check their main circuit breaker before reporting an outage. Oʻahu customers can use the company’s online outage reporting service or contact the Oʻahu Trouble Line at 1-855-304-1212. Residents should continue to avoid damaged electrical equipment and treat any downed power line as dangerous.

The numbers are a snapshot and can change as crews complete repairs or identify additional localized damage. For PinoyLink Hawaiʻi readers, the practical takeaway is that most storm-related Oʻahu outages have been restored, while a smaller number of customers may still need utility or property-level repairs before service returns.

stories.headline: Manny Pacquiao takes Cabinet-level anti-poverty post
stories.summary: Former senator Manny Pacquiao has taken his oath as Secretary and Lead Convenor of the National Anti-Poverty Commission, returning to Philippine government service in a Cabinet-level role.
stories.why_it_matters: NAPC coordinates and advises on national poverty-reduction and social-reform programs, making the leadership change relevant to Filipino families following government assistance and development policy.
stories.source_name: Philippine News Agency / Presidential Communications Office
body: Former senator and boxing champion Manny Pacquiao has returned to Philippine government service as Secretary and Lead Convenor of the National Anti-Poverty Commission. Pacquiao took his oath before President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. at Malacañang on Tuesday, September 8, according to the Philippine News Agency and the Presidential Communications Office.

The appointment places Pacquiao at the head of the NAPC secretariat with Cabinet rank under Republic Act No. 8425, the Social Reform and Poverty Alleviation Act. He succeeds Lope Santos III. The commission serves as a coordinating and advisory body for the government’s social-reform and poverty-alleviation agenda rather than functioning as a stand-alone benefits program.

NAPC’s mandate includes coordinating anti-poverty programs among national agencies, local governments and the private sector; monitoring implementation; recommending policy measures; and helping basic sectors participate in policymaking. The commission also works on the National Anti-Poverty Action Agenda, which provides a framework for government interventions across social, economic, ecological and governance dimensions.

Pacquiao’s appointment marks his first government post since his Senate term ended in June 2022. He previously served six years in the Senate and earlier represented Sarangani in the House of Representatives. His new role shifts his public-service focus toward coordination of poverty-reduction and social-reform policy.

For Filipinos in Hawaiʻi with family members in the Philippines, the immediate significance is institutional rather than a new individual entitlement: the appointment changes the leadership of the national body that coordinates poverty-alleviation strategy. Any future program, eligibility or assistance changes should be verified through the responsible Philippine government agency before families act on them.

stories.headline: Farrington Highway fully reopened after Lowell cleanup
stories.summary: HDOT says all lanes at Hakimo Road and between Lualualei Naval Road and Helelua Street reopened Tuesday evening, and Oʻahu special-use lanes including the Nānākuli contraflow are expected to operate normally for the rest of the week.
stories.why_it_matters: West Oʻahu commuters can plan Wednesday travel with the major storm-related Farrington Highway restrictions cleared, while recovery work continues elsewhere in the state.
body: A major storm-related traffic restriction on Oʻahu’s Leeward Coast has been cleared. The Hawaiʻi Department of Transportation said all lanes of Farrington Highway at Hakimo Road and between Lualualei Naval Road and Helelua Street reopened at 6:30 p.m. Tuesday after crews removed sand and debris left by Hurricane Lowell.

The reopening is an important step toward a more normal Wednesday commute for West Oʻahu. HDOT also said Oʻahu special-use lanes, including the Nānākuli contraflow, will operate normally for the remainder of the week. The corridor had been disrupted after high surf and storm conditions pushed water, sand and debris onto portions of the highway.

Drivers should still use extra care in areas affected by the storm. Cleanup and recovery work can continue near shoulders, coastal access points and local streets even after the main highway reopens. Conditions can also change after additional showers, so motorists should watch for crews, debris and temporary traffic controls.

Elsewhere in the state, transportation recovery remains uneven. HDOT reported continuing work on Kauaʻi and Maui and said some harbor operations were still affected Tuesday evening. For Oʻahu commuters, however, the agency’s latest update confirms that the previously restricted Farrington Highway segments are open and the normal special-use lane schedule is expected to resume.

stories.headline: Oʻahu schools, offices and UH reopen Wednesday after Lowell
stories.summary: State and county offices, public schools, UH campuses and Judiciary facilities on Oʻahu reopen Sept. 9 as conditions improve following Hurricane Lowell.
stories.why_it_matters: Families, students and workers on Oʻahu can resume normal schedules Wednesday, while anyone coordinating with Kauaʻi should expect continued storm-recovery disruptions.
stories.source_name: Office of the Governor, State of Hawaiʻi
body: Oʻahu is returning to a more normal schedule Wednesday after Hurricane Lowell moved away from the Hawaiian Islands. Governor Josh Green announced that state and county offices, Hawaiʻi Department of Education public schools, University of Hawaiʻi campuses and state Judiciary facilities on Oʻahu will reopen September 9.

The reopening follows Tuesday closures that were ordered while Lowell brought dangerous winds, rain, flooding and surf to parts of the state. Officials said conditions on Oʻahu improved enough to resume operations, although cleanup and utility restoration work continues in some communities.

Public schools and offices in Maui County and on Hawaiʻi Island are also reopening Wednesday, including four West Maui schools that had closed because of unsafe travel conditions. Kauaʻi remains the major exception: state and county offices and Kauaʻi Community College are expected to remain closed through Friday, September 11, while crews restore power and clear debris. Public schools on Kauaʻi and Niʻihau are also remaining closed to students through Friday.

Oʻahu residents should still allow extra time for travel where localized cleanup is underway and should continue checking agency notices for individual facilities or services. The statewide emergency response is shifting toward recovery, but conditions and restoration timelines differ significantly by island.

stories.headline: Lowell impacts continue across Hawaiʻi as storm moves away
stories.summary: Hurricane Lowell is moving away from the islands, but dangerous surf, heavy rain and strong winds remain concerns across parts of Hawaiʻi through Tuesday.
stories.why_it_matters: Oʻahu commuters, coastal communities, travelers and families should continue checking official weather and emergency guidance before heading out.

stories.headline: Farrington Highway closure affects West Oʻahu
stories.summary: Honolulu Police closed Farrington Highway in both directions between Princess Kahanu Avenue and Kaukama Road after hazardous high surf sent waves across all four lanes.
stories.why_it_matters: The closure directly affects Waiʻanae Coast travel and may cause significant detours and delays for residents, workers and emergency access.

stories.headline: Habagat continues to affect Luzon and the Visayas
stories.summary: PAGASA says the Southwest Monsoon is affecting Luzon and the Visayas, bringing rain to western sections and scattered thunderstorms to other areas.
stories.why_it_matters: Families in Hawaiʻi with relatives traveling or living in affected Philippine regions should watch for localized flooding, landslides and transportation disruptions.

stories.summary: PinoyLink Hawaiʻi is building a Filipino community newsroom connecting island life with trusted updates from home.
stories.why_it_matters: The goal is to give Hawaiʻi readers one practical place for local news, Philippines updates, immigration information, community events, jobs, business and opportunities.
